title: How your nose reads the air
description: You carry around four hundred kinds of scent sensors, and together they can distinguish a staggering variety of smells — including ones that unlock memories.

body.heading: A patch of sensors the size of a stamp
paragraphs: High inside your nose sits a small patch of tissue, only a few centimetres across, packed with millions of smell receptor cells. Humans have about 400 different types of these receptors, each one responding to particular shapes and features of airborne molecules.

No single receptor identifies a smell by itself. Instead, each scent activates a pattern across many receptors, like a chord played on a piano, and your brain learns to recognise the chord. With 400 keys, the number of possible chords is enormous.

body.heading: Why flavour is mostly smell
paragraphs: Much of what you call taste is actually smell. Your tongue detects only a handful of basics — sweet, salty, sour, bitter, savoury — while your nose, working from behind your mouth as you chew, supplies the rich detail that makes a strawberry different from a raspberry.
This is why food tastes dull when you have a blocked nose. The tongue is doing its job as usual; the orchestra behind it has gone quiet.

body.heading: The memory connection
paragraphs: Smell has a unusually direct line to the parts of the brain involved in emotion and memory. That is why the smell of rain on hot pavement or a particular soap can return a childhood afternoon to you whole, before you have time to think about it.
Scientists are still mapping exactly how the brain builds these links. Your nose, meanwhile, keeps quietly reading the air — and filing the memories away.

takeaway: Smell works by pattern: about 400 receptor types play chords your brain recognises, flavours, and files away as memories.
